verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For ContentKing, schedule a modest owned-site crawl and alert on selected technical changes. The hard boundary is continuous monitoring infrastructure, prioritization, integrations, and enterprise scale, plus crawl scale, rule depth, and operational polish.
coreLoopDIY: Schedule a modest crawl of a user-owned site, inspect HTML and rendered pages, alert on selected technical changes, explain prioritized issues, and export a reproducible audit.
requirements: permission to crawl the target site
whatYouLose: continuous monitoring infrastructure, prioritization, integrations, and enterprise scale
moatNotes: crawl scale, rule depth, and operational polish
ongoingBurden: robots handling, rendering, canonicalization, deduplication, crawl traps, rule maintenance, scheduling, storage, and false positives
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for ContentKing because a crawler is buildable; professionals pay for years of edge-case handling and reports they can trust with clients. The recurring cost buys robots handling, rendering, canonicalization, deduplication, crawl traps, rule maintenance, scheduling, storage, and false positives, not just the visible interface.

alternatives.name: CrawlSEO
alternatives.desc: Scheduled crawls and real alerts without a subscription; the catch is configuring Google OAuth, Postgres and notification plumbing yourself.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Custom plan and a single-site audit tool DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for ContentKing in an empty repository.
Use Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLite, Playwright, and an HTMX interface; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: schedule a modest crawl of a user-owned site, inspect HTML and rendered pages, alert on selected technical changes, explain prioritized issues, and export a reproducible audit.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Require an explicit ownership or permission acknowledgement before a crawl starts.
Respect robots.txt, rate limits, canonical URLs, nofollow, redirects, and a configurable URL cap.
Collect status, title, description, headings, canonical, robots, links, images, structured data, and rendered text.
Detect duplicates, orphan candidates, broken links, redirect chains, missing metadata, and indexability conflicts.
Show every issue with affected URLs, evidence, severity, and a concrete remediation note.
Export crawl data and issues to CSV plus a self-contained HTML report.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out crawling sites without permission.
Deliberately leave out web-scale backlink or keyword datasets.
Deliberately leave out automated changes to production websites.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
